newsitem.title: USA: Justice distances itself from Thompson charge.
newsitem.headline: Justice distances itself from Thompson charge.

text.p: The Justice Department has distanced itself from Sen. Fred Thompson's charge that the Chinese government plotted to increase their influence over the U.S. political process, a letter showed Sunday.
The Justice Department letter to Thompson, quoted on ABC's "This Week" program, said that any conclusions the senator drew were his own and not necessarily those of Justice.

Thompson opened the hearings on campaign fund raising -- scheduled to last for months -- with a surprising and sweeping accusation that "the committee believes that high-level Chinese government officials crafted a plan to increase China's influence over the U.S. political process."

Thompson said his view was based on secret documents, many provided by the Justice Department. But Assistant Attorney General Andrew Fois wrote Thompson to make it clear the department had not signed on to the senator's views.
"You neither requested nor received assessments of the accuracy of any conclusions you drew from information available to the committee," said the letter. "Those conclusions of course are your own."

Sen. John Glenn, an Ohio Democrat and the ranking Democrat on the Senate Government Affairs Committee, read from the letter on the ABC show and said he disagreed with Thompson's assessment of the classified intelligence data.

"I would not have gone as far as Sen. Thompson did in describing the situation," he said. "I've read all the same reports that he has read." Glenn said they received information from both the Justice Department and the CIA.

"He swung a broader loop on some of the conclusions than I would swing. I'll just leave it at that," Glenn said, repeating his criticism that Thompson was running the hearings and controlling subpoenas in a partisan manner.

But Thompson, speaking on NBC's "Meet the Press" program, defended his assertion, saying, "I would not go out and make a statement like this if it was not on solid ground and if I had not had the opportunity to let some people see this before I did it, and proceed in that fashion."

But he cautioned that the investigation was ongoing and it was impossible to know at this point exactly which players would still be subpoenaed to testify -- or what the final outcome of the hearing would be.
Thompson denied that the hearings were focused solely on Democratic fund-raising abuses:
"There's no allegation here that this was all towards the Democrats, by any means," he said. "There's no allegation that it was all presidential. In fact, most of it ... was congressional."
"It was a broad situation that involved all levels," the Tennessee Republican said.

"Everybody needs to just kind of take a deep breath and settle down a little bit ... it's a building block approach," he said. "These hearings are not soap operas designed to titillate. They're not athletic events where we keep a running score."

Thompson's opening statement also appeared to be undercut by a story in U.S. News & World Report. The report quoted the FBI as suggesting that a crucial link was missing between alleged Chinese efforts to exert influence and an effort by Democrats to raise money from Asians.

"There was a campaign by the Chinese to infiltrate Congress and a campaign by the Democrats to gain contributions from wealthy Asian-Americans," the magazine quoted the FBI official as saying. "Were the two linked? Where's the proof?"
Asked the same question, Thompson said, "Well, we're not ready to deal with that yet ... I don't know if we'll ever have the answer to that question."
Thompson said it remained to be seen if the two efforts were part of a plan by the Chinese government.

"We may never know the answer to that, or we may have to have prosecutions later on and have some people convicted who are then willing to talk before we really ever find the answer to that," he said.

The hearings are scheduled to end Dec. 31, but Thompson said he might seek an extension if there was more work to be done. "We've got an awful lot of territory to cover. The investigation is ongoing," he said.
Thompson also denied using the hearings as a platform to launch a bid for the Republican presidential nomination in 2000, although he declined to explicitly rule out a run for the White House.
